name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
powers: Shrinks and grows at the wearer's will; weighs thirteen thousand five hundred catties
description: Ruyi Jingu Bang is the magic staff of Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the great Chinese novel Journey to the West, and it is counted among the most famous weapons in all of Asian literature. The staff began as the great pillar of the Eastern Sea Dragon Palace, a golden-banded rod weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties, which no one could lift until the Monkey King took it up and found it shrank and grew at his will, from a needle kept in his ear to a pillar that could reach the clouds. With it Sun Wukong defied the heavenly host, fought the armies of the Jade Emperor, and later escorted the monk Tripitaka to the West, the staff serving as both weapon and staff of office. The weapon's name is often translated as 'the complaisant golden cudgel' or 'wish-fulfilling staff,' and its image is inseparable from the character who wields it. Ruyi Jingu Bang appears throughout the sequel novel and in opera, film, and games, and remains the emblem of the irrepressible Monkey King.

name: Jiu Ding
powers: Signifies the Mandate of Heaven and legitimacy of rule
description: The jiu ding are the nine bronze tripods that the culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces after he tamed the great flood, inscribing each region's creatures and things on the sides so that the people could recognize them. Passed down through the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography, and losing them was read as the fall of a dynasty. No actual ding survive, and their very existence is a matter of debate, but the story carried enormous political weight: Confucius, Mencius, and the historian Sima Qian all allude to the tripods as the vessels of sovereignty. In the Warring States tale of the King of Chu who 'asked about the tripods' at the Zhou court, the sheer idea of the ding became a test of ambition. The jiu ding remain the standard Chinese symbol of rightful imperial power and of the unity of the realm.

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of Hou Yi is the weapon of the legendary archer of Chinese myth who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth, leaving a single sun to light the day. Each of the ten suns was the child of the goddess Xihe, and when all ten rose together the world began to burn; Hou Yi, a peerless bowman, felled nine of them with arrows tipped against the sun-birds that drew the solar chariot. In the same cycle of tales his skill earned him the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it and drifted to the moon, and the archer was left behind. The bow therefore stands for the archetypal marksman and for the human cost of divine power, and Hou Yi is invoked across Chinese literature whenever perfect archery is described. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources and echoed in the poem 'Tianwen', gives the bow a permanent place among the weapons of Chinese mythology.

name: Elixir of Immortality
description: The elixir of immortality is the drug of eternal life that the Queen Mother of the West, Xiwangmu, is said to have kept in her paradise of Kunlun, and it is the pivot of one of the most famous tales in Chinese mythology. The archer Hou Yi obtained the elixir as a reward for shooting down the nine suns, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief, and was lifted to the moon where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources such as Huainanzi, gave the moon its goddess, and the jade rabbit that pounds herbs in a mortar is her companion on the lunar surface. In later Daoist tradition the elixir became the goal of alchemy, both as a physical drug of cinnabar and gold and as an inner refinement of the body's energies. The story anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when offerings of mooncakes recall Chang'e's flight, and the elixir remains the standard image of the Daoist quest for transcendence.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality is a fixed image in the Chinese moon, the rabbit standing beside the cassia tree on the lunar surface as the companion of the goddess Chang'e. In the Moon Rabbit folklore, the rabbit first earned its place when it offered itself as food to a disguised deity, who spared it and set it on the moon to grind the herbs of immortality, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore. In Korea the rabbit is said to pound the ingredients of the rice cake tteok, while in Japan it pounds mochi, and in Vietnam it is the companion of the moon goddess Hang Nga. The mortar is depicted in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery on lanterns, mooncakes, and shadow-puppets, and the figure of the rabbit at work is one of the most recognizable of the moon's markings. Across all these traditions the mortar turns the mundane labour of grinding grain into the cosmic work of producing the elixir of life.
source: Han bronze mirrors and moon-rabbit tradition

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: The bagua mirror is a circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy, sha qi, and to return an attacker's evil gaze. In domestic use it is placed above the main door or facing a threatening structure such as a road, a corner, or a neighbour's roof-ridge, so that the mirror deflects or reflects the influence back to its source. The mirror also appears in Daoist talismanic practice, paired with written spells against hauntings and possession, and the convex form is said to disperse harm while the concave form gathers or focuses it. Because of its power to reflect, the bagua mirror is one of the few feng shui remedies that practitioners advise using with care, lest the mirrored effect fall on an innocent. The object joins the practical science of geomancy to the older Chinese belief in mirrors as revealers of spirits, a connection that goes back to the bronze mirrors of the Han period.

name: Guan Dao
material: Steel blade on a long wooden shaft
powers: Emblem of martial protection and the god of war
description: The guan dao is the heavy curved-blade polearm historically associated with Guan Yu, the great general of the Three Kingdoms period who was deified as the god of war and of righteousness, and its most famous example is the Green Dragon Crescent Blade. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms Guan Yu carries the enormous weapon, and in legend the blade was so heavy that only he could wield it; temples honouring him display a ceremonial guan dao in his image, and the weapon became a standard of the military temples and of martial artists. The actual historical guan dao developed later than the general's lifetime, and the famous blade is a literary creation, but the association made the weapon a fixture of Chinese and East Asian iconography. In the folk tradition a guan dao kept in a home or temple is thought to carry Guan Yu's protective presence, and it is still carried in lion-dance performances and temple processions. The blade's name has passed into popular culture across the world as the emblem of the bearded warrior-saint.

name: Flaming Pearl
description: The flaming pearl, huozhu, is a luminous orb wreathed in curling flame that Chinese art shows two dragons chasing or guarding, and it is one of the most common motifs of East Asian decoration. The image appears on temple roofs, ceramic dishes, paintings, and lanterns, and its meaning draws on several layers: in Buddhist iconography the pearl is the cintamani, the wish-granting jewel that fulfils every desire, while in Daoist cosmology it can stand for the moon, the sun, or the inner pearl of spiritual refinement. The dragon that guards the pearl is usually the celestial dragon of rain and water, and the chase motif is sometimes read as the play of yin and yang or of the sun and moon across the heavens. In folk belief the pearl is also linked to the treasure of the dragon's undersea palace, and stories tell of heroes who descend to the sea king's court for the jewel. Whatever the reading, the flaming pearl carries a consistent charge of wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it remains the standard companion of the dragon in pan-Asian art.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The heavenly loom is the celestial weaving frame of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who in Chinese myth wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River, the Milky Way. When she married the cowherd Niulang and neglected her weaving, the Jade Emperor or the Queen Mother of the West separated the pair across the river, allowing them to meet only once a year; on the seventh night of the seventh month, magpies form a bridge over the river and the lovers reunite. The tale, first recorded in Han-era poetry, became the origin of the Qixi festival, the Chinese Valentine's day, when girls pray to Zhinü for skill in needlework and for love. The loom is thus the engine of the sky's patterned beauty and the emblem of the craft that the festival celebrates. The same story is told in Korea as Chilseok and in Japan as Tanabata, where the weaving goddess Orihime is remembered with strips of paper hung on bamboo.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources
